newsitem.title: GERMANY: Dasa keeps up pressure on Eurofighter.
newsitem.headline: Dasa keeps up pressure on Eurofighter.

text.p: Dasa, the lossmaking aerospace arm of Germany's Daimler-Benz AG, turned up the pressure on Tuesday on the Bonn government to make a firm order for Eurofighter combat aircraft this year.

Dasa board member Dietrich Russell said at an evening event that the costs of serial production of the four-country Eurofighter project could escalate if Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government delays committing itself to full-scale production.
"Delays will increase the costs of the whole programme and force the offer to be reviewed," Russell said at the opening of an aerospace exhibition outside Bonn.
Defence Minister Volker Ruehe wants to buy 180 Eurofighters out of a planned total first production run of 620 aircraft.

But his ministry still wants price cuts before it seeks legislative approval for the purchase. Parliament is expected to discuss buying Eurofighter as part of 1997 budget debates expected to wind up in November, a ministry spokesman said.
Dasa has a 30 percent stake in the Eurofighter project, with British Aerospace holding 37.5 percent, Alenia SpA on 19 percent and Spain's CASA with 13 percent.
The group put a revised offer to Germany earlier this year -- details of which have not been published.

But the spokesman said the price for a single fighter would have to be "substantially lower" than the 133 million marks originally proposed for a higher-specification original version of the Eurofighter back in 1991 -- plus inflation costs.
The spokesman said that Eurofighter was the ministry's top procurement priority and warned that if it does get approval other weapons purchase programmes may have to be cut.
Russell said that 18,000 highly-qualified jobs in Germany alone hang on the multi-billion mark Eurofighter project.

More is at stake, Russell added, in maintaining Germany's aerospace industry as a viable partner in Europe-wide military aircraft projects -- which are becoming increasingly difficult to finance as the costs of state-of-the-art technology soar.
"Because of high development costs the next generation will definitely be common European projects," Russell said.
He said that a military transport aircraft project being developed by the Airbus consortium represented one opportunity.
He said he would also welcome Westland of Great Britain and Agusta of Italy to join the Eurocopter group -- a 60/40 joint venture between France's Aerospatiale and Dasa.
A Dasa spokesman was unable to confirm whether any concrete talks had been held with Westland and Agusta on Eurocopter.
